books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of the account of the Panic of 1857 in Wikipedia, “Panic of 1857,” and civilwar.com, “The Crash of 1857,” consulted 2026-11-26. The Panic of 1857 is not covered in the three books’ Topic 5.6 sections; the facts here were verified against those two secondary sources. The wording is original.
stimulus.text: Paraphrase: In August 1857, the Ohio Life Insurance and Trust Company failed, and the panic spread fast: banks stopped paying out gold, railroad stocks fell, and more than 5,000 American businesses failed within a year. The North’s factories and railroads suffered most, while the South’s cotton trade stayed strong, and Southerners pointed to the panic as proof that their slave economy was sounder than Northern free labor.

rationales.A: The passage says the opposite: the South’s cotton trade stayed strong while the North suffered.
rationales.B: Gold mining is not in the passage; the panic struck banks, railroads, and factories.
rationales.C: Settlement is not in the passage; the panic struck the settled North’s banks and railroads.
rationales.D: The failed bank, the fallen railroad stocks, and the 5,000 failed businesses were Northern, while Southern cotton held its price.
rationales.general:
1. Follow the failures: an Ohio bank, then banks, railroads, and businesses across the North.
2. Count the damage: more than 5,000 businesses failed within a year.
3. Compare the South: its cotton trade stayed strong, so the panic looked like a Northern disease.
4. Note the spark: the Ohio Life Insurance and Trust Company failed on August 24, 1857, and the panic spread from there.
Remember: a panic that strikes one section and spares the other becomes a political argument.
